lines.text: Two numbers have a least common multiple of seventy-two. How many such pairs are there?
lines.caption: Two numbers have a least common multiple of seventy-two. How many such pairs are there?

lines.text: Most kids find a few pairs, then guess. <short pause> There are more than you would think!
lines.caption: Most kids find a few pairs, then guess. There are more than you would think!

lines.text: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count them all together.
lines.caption: Hi, I'm Vantee! Let's count them all together.

lines.text: Here's the question.
lines.caption: Here's the question.

lines.text: How many ordered pairs of positive whole numbers
lines.caption: How many ordered pairs of positive whole numbers

lines.text: have least common multiple seventy-two?
lines.caption: have least common multiple seventy-two?

lines.text: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.
lines.caption: Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

lines.text: So what's a least common multiple? It's the smallest number that both a and b go into.
lines.caption: So what's a least common multiple? It's the smallest number that both a and b go into.

lines.text: Take eight and nine. The smallest number they both go into is seventy-two. So that pair counts!
lines.caption: Take eight and nine. The smallest number they both go into is seventy-two. So that pair counts!

lines.text: Ordered means order matters. Eight, nine and nine, eight are two DIFFERENT pairs.
lines.caption: Ordered means order matters. Eight, nine and nine, eight are two DIFFERENT pairs.

lines.text: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!
lines.caption: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

lines.text: Welcome back! Since a and b both go into seventy-two, each one is a divisor of seventy-two.
lines.caption: Welcome back! Since a and b both go into seventy-two, each one is a divisor of seventy-two.

lines.text: Seventy-two is eight times nine. That's two times two times two, times three times three.
lines.caption: Seventy-two is eight times nine. That's two times two times two, times three times three.

lines.text: Let's put all twelve divisors in a table. Powers of two go across, and powers of three go down.
lines.caption: Let's put all twelve divisors in a table. Powers of two go across, and powers of three go down.

lines.text: Here's the trick. Seventy-two has three twos. One number must bring all three: a multiple of eight.
lines.caption: Here's the trick. Seventy-two has three twos. One number must bring all three: a multiple of eight.

lines.text: Seventy-two has two threes, too. So one number must bring both: a multiple of nine.
lines.caption: Seventy-two has two threes, too. So one number must bring both: a multiple of nine.

lines.text: Say a is twelve. It's not a multiple of eight or nine. So b must be both. Only seventy-two works!
lines.caption: Say a is twelve. It's not a multiple of eight or nine. So b must be both. Only seventy-two works!

lines.text: Say a is eight. Then b only needs to be a multiple of nine.
lines.caption: Say a is eight. Then b only needs to be a multiple of nine.

lines.text: That's nine, eighteen, thirty-six or seventy-two. That makes four partners!
lines.caption: That's nine, eighteen, thirty-six or seventy-two. That makes four partners!

lines.text: If a is seventy-two, it brings everything. So b can be any of the twelve divisors!
lines.caption: If a is seventy-two, it brings everything. So b can be any of the twelve divisors!

lines.text: Twelve and these five others aren't multiples of eight or nine. One partner each.
lines.caption: Twelve and these five others aren't multiples of eight or nine. One partner each.

lines.text: Eight and twenty-four are multiples of eight, but not nine. Four partners each.
lines.caption: Eight and twenty-four are multiples of eight, but not nine. Four partners each.

lines.text: Nine, eighteen and thirty-six need eight, twenty-four or seventy-two. Three partners each.
lines.caption: Nine, eighteen and thirty-six need eight, twenty-four or seventy-two. Three partners each.

lines.text: Now add. The top row is one plus one plus one plus four, which is seven. So is the middle row.
lines.caption: Now add. The top row is one plus one plus one plus four, which is seven. So is the middle row.

lines.text: The bottom row is three plus three plus three plus twelve. That's twenty-one.
lines.caption: The bottom row is three plus three plus three plus twelve. That's twenty-one.

lines.text: Seven plus seven plus twenty-one is thirty-five! The answer is D.
lines.caption: Seven plus seven plus twenty-one is thirty-five! The answer is D.

scenes.chapter: Solution 2: one prime at a time

lines.text: Now for a second way. Let's look at the twos and the threes separately.
lines.caption: Now for a second way. Let's look at the twos and the threes separately.

lines.text: Take eight and eighteen. Eight has three twos and no threes. Eighteen has one two and two threes.
lines.caption: Take eight and eighteen. Eight has three twos and no threes. Eighteen has one two and two threes.

lines.text: Their least common multiple keeps the most of each: three twos and two threes. That's seventy-two!
lines.caption: Their least common multiple keeps the most of each: three twos and two threes. That's seventy-two!

lines.text: Let's make a grid for the twos. Across is how many twos a has: zero, one, two or three.
lines.caption: Let's make a grid for the twos. Across is how many twos a has: zero, one, two or three.

lines.text: Down is how many twos b has. Four by four makes sixteen squares.
lines.caption: Down is how many twos b has. Four by four makes sixteen squares.

lines.text: The most twos must be three. So at least one of a and b has three twos.
lines.caption: The most twos must be three. So at least one of a and b has three twos.

lines.text: That's the last column and the bottom row. Four plus four, but the corner is in both. Seven!
lines.caption: That's the last column and the bottom row. Four plus four, but the corner is in both. Seven!

lines.text: Let's double-check. The top-left three by three block has no three. Sixteen minus nine is seven.
lines.caption: Let's double-check. The top-left three by three block has no three. Sixteen minus nine is seven.

lines.text: Now the threes. Each of a and b has zero, one or two threes. That's a three by three grid.
lines.caption: Now the threes. Each of a and b has zero, one or two threes. That's a three by three grid.

lines.text: At least one needs two threes. Three plus three, minus the corner, is five. Or nine minus four!
lines.caption: At least one needs two threes. Three plus three, minus the corner, is five. Or nine minus four!

lines.text: Any way for the twos can go with any way for the threes. Like seven shirts and five pairs of pants.
lines.caption: Any way for the twos can go with any way for the threes. Like seven shirts and five pairs of pants.

lines.text: Seven times five is thirty-five. Same answer!
lines.caption: Seven times five is thirty-five. Same answer!

lines.text: When would you pick this way? When the number is big, and the table would get huge.
lines.caption: When would you pick this way? When the number is big, and the table would get huge.

lines.text: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.
lines.caption: Now let's look at the wrong answers. Each one is a trap.

lines.text: Twelve counts the divisors of seventy-two. But we're counting pairs, not single numbers.
lines.caption: Twelve counts the divisors of seventy-two. But we're counting pairs, not single numbers.

lines.text: Eighteen is what you'd get if order didn't matter. Then eight, nine and nine, eight are one pair.
lines.caption: Eighteen is what you'd get if order didn't matter. Then eight, nine and nine, eight are one pair.

lines.text: Every pair has a twin, except seventy-two, seventy-two. Thirty-four over two, plus one, is eighteen.
lines.caption: Every pair has a twin, except seventy-two, seventy-two. Thirty-four over two, plus one, is eighteen.

lines.text: Twenty-four is what you'd get if you doubled the twelve divisors. But eight alone has four partners!
lines.caption: Twenty-four is what you'd get if you doubled the twelve divisors. But eight alone has four partners!

lines.text: Seventy is what you'd get if you doubled thirty-five to handle order. But we already counted both orders.
lines.caption: Seventy is what you'd get if you doubled thirty-five to handle order. But we already counted both orders.

lines.text: So here's a great habit. Before you count, ask: does order matter? Here, it does!
lines.caption: So here's a great habit. Before you count, ask: does order matter? Here, it does!

lines.text: Ready for a challenge? Here's a new one.
lines.caption: Ready for a challenge? Here's a new one.

lines.text: How many ordered pairs of positive whole numbers
lines.caption: How many ordered pairs of positive whole numbers

lines.text: have least common multiple forty-eight?
lines.caption: have least common multiple forty-eight?

lines.text: Pause the video, and go for it!
lines.caption: Pause the video, and go for it!

lines.text: Let's check. Forty-eight is sixteen times three. That's four twos and one three.
lines.caption: Let's check. Forty-eight is sixteen times three. That's four twos and one three.

lines.text: For the twos, each of a and b has zero to four. That's a five by five grid, twenty-five squares.
lines.caption: For the twos, each of a and b has zero to four. That's a five by five grid, twenty-five squares.

lines.text: The misses have fewer than four twos: a four by four block. Twenty-five minus sixteen is nine.
lines.caption: The misses have fewer than four twos: a four by four block. Twenty-five minus sixteen is nine.

lines.text: For the threes, it's zero or one. Two by two is four, minus one miss. That's three.
lines.caption: For the threes, it's zero or one. Two by two is four, minus one miss. That's three.

lines.text: Nine times three is twenty-seven! If you found it, amazing work!
lines.caption: Nine times three is twenty-seven! If you found it, amazing work!

lines.text: Here's the big idea. For each prime, the least common multiple keeps the bigger of the two powers.
lines.caption: Here's the big idea. For each prime, the least common multiple keeps the bigger of the two powers.

lines.text: So make a grid of powers for each prime, count the good squares, then multiply.
lines.caption: So make a grid of powers for each prime, count the good squares, then multiply.

lines.text: I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
lines.caption: I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
